explanations.explanation: Honor is the word. The LORD says, "A son honors his father, and a servant his master." He starts with something every person already understands, and then turns it on the priests. When your own example is that easy to follow, it's hard to dodge the question.

The verse never brings up wages. The LORD says, "A son honors his father, and a servant his master." Nobody's checking a paycheck here, because a son doesn't send his dad an invoice. The thing in view is honor.

Gifts are a nice guess, since the priests are offering things at an altar. But in this verse the LORD names honor, not gifts: "A son honors his father, and a servant his master." Then He asks, "where is My honor?" The question is about how they treat Him, not what they hand over.
Defiled is right. The LORD says they present "defiled food on My altar." The altar is where the offerings should be holy, so this stings. Then they ask how they defiled Him, and He keeps answering.

Leftover is a reasonable guess, but that isn't the word the LORD uses. He says the priests present defiled food on His altar. Leftover cookies from Tuesday are still cookies, so I can see why it sounds mild. Defiled is a much heavier word.

Borrowed isn't in the verse. The LORD says the priests present defiled food on His altar. Nothing in the text says they got it from anybody else. The problem He names is the condition of the food, not where it came from.
True. The LORD says they've defiled Him "By saying that the table of the LORD is contemptible." So it wasn't only what they put on the altar. It was also what they said about it.
The text says the opposite. The LORD answers their question by naming it: "By saying that the table of the LORD is contemptible." The priests were calling His table contemptible, and He heard it.

True. The LORD says, "Try offering them to your governor!" Then He asks if the governor would be pleased or show favor. It's like showing up to your boss's party with a busted lamp and calling it a gift. The priests already know how that would go.

The LORD really does say it. After naming the blind, lame and sick animals, He says, "Try offering them to your governor!" Then He asks, "Would he be pleased with you or show you favor?" He sends them to a human official to make His point.

Useless is the word. The LORD says He wishes someone would shut the doors "so that you would no longer kindle useless fires on My altar!" Fires that should mean something are going to waste. I'd say that's a heavy thing to hear.

Foreign isn't the word here. The LORD says He wants the doors shut so the priests would "no longer kindle useless fires on My altar!" The fires belong to His altar, and the problem is that they're useless. Nothing in the verse points to outside fires.
Morning sounds tidy, but the verse doesn't say it. The LORD wants the doors shut so they would "no longer kindle useless fires on My altar!" The word is useless. Time of day never comes up.
The text says no. The LORD says, "I take no pleasure in you," and then, "I will accept no offering from your hands." It's a closed door. That's why He'd rather the temple doors be shut.

False is right. The LORD says, "I take no pleasure in you," and "I will accept no offering from your hands." So these offerings aren't getting through. Better to shut the doors than keep lighting fires He won't accept.

Nations is right. The LORD says, "My name will be great among the nations, from where the sun rises to where it sets." That's a much bigger picture than one temple. Pure offerings will be presented in His name in every place.

It's a natural guess, since the LORD has been talking to the priests this whole time. But He says His name will be great among the nations. The priests are the ones who despise it, and He points past them. His name stays great anyway.

Elders don't appear in this verse. The LORD says, "My name will be great among the nations." He's looking far from this one altar, from where the sun rises to where it sets. The word you want is nations.

explanations.answer: They turn up their nose at it
explanations.explanation: That's it. The LORD says, "you turn up your nose at it." It's the face of someone who just opened a gym bag. And the thing getting that face is His table.

explanations.answer: They bow down low before it
explanations.explanation: That's the opposite of what the text says. The LORD says the priests "turn up your nose at it." Nobody is bowing here. They're sniffing at the LORD's table like it's beneath them.

Nobody's weeping in these verses. The LORD says they say, "Oh, what a nuisance!" and "you turn up your nose at it." That's complaining and contempt, not sorrow. I'd say a quiet cry would have been easier to hear.
True. The LORD says, "You bring offerings that are stolen, lame, or sick!" So the list gets longer than just hurt animals. Then He asks, "Should I accept these from your hands?"
The text says it plainly. The LORD says, "You bring offerings that are stolen, lame, or sick!" Stolen is right there with lame and sick. Then He asks if He should accept these from their hands.

A defective animal is right. The man has an acceptable male in his flock and vows to give it. Then he "sacrifices a defective animal to the Lord." The good one stays home and the broken one goes to the altar.

Wild animals don't show up in the verse. The man has an acceptable male in his flock and vows to give it. What he actually sacrifices is a defective animal. The text is about a swap within his own flock.

The text doesn't talk about age. It says the man vows to give the acceptable male but "sacrifices a defective animal to the Lord." Defective is the word, not young. The swap is about the condition of the animal.
King is the word. The LORD says, "For I am a great King," and "My name is to be feared among the nations." That follows the curse on the deceiver. The One being cheated is the great King.
Shepherd fits since the verse has a flock in it. But the LORD says, "For I am a great King." And He adds that His name is to be feared among the nations. King is the word that's there.
Builder doesn't appear in this verse. The LORD says, "For I am a great King," and His name is to be feared among the nations. No hammers, no blueprints. The word is King.
Blessings is right. The LORD says, "I will send a curse among you, and I will curse your blessings." That's a serious one. Even the good things they have fall under it.
Harvests are a sensible guess, but the verse doesn't say it. The LORD says, "I will send a curse among you, and I will curse your blessings." The word is blessings. He doesn't name any crop.

Households aren't mentioned in this verse. The LORD says, "I will send a curse among you, and I will curse your blessings." The word you're looking for is blessings. The text doesn't say which blessings.
True. The LORD says, "Yes, I have already begun to curse them, because you are not taking it to heart." So this isn't only a warning about later. It has already started.

The text says otherwise. The LORD says, "Yes, I have already begun to curse them, because you are not taking it to heart." It's already begun. The "if" in the verse before it is not only about the future.

explanations.answer: He stood in awe of His name
explanations.explanation: That's right. The LORD says the covenant "called for reverence, and he revered Me and stood in awe of My name." Levi, whose name the priests' tribe carries, did what the covenant asked. That's the standard the priests are being measured against.

explanations.answer: He grew weary of His ways
explanations.explanation: Being weary is closer to what the priests are doing, not Levi. The LORD says of Levi, "he revered Me and stood in awe of My name." Levi, whose name the priests' tribe carries, answered the covenant with reverence. No tired sighing from him.

explanations.answer: He drifted far from His call
explanations.explanation: The text says the opposite about Levi. The LORD says, "He walked with Me in peace and uprightness." And the covenant "called for reverence, and he revered Me and stood in awe of My name." The drifting is what the LORD says the priests have done.
The text says more than that. The LORD says Levi "turned many from iniquity." Not a few. The number is many.
False is right. The LORD says of Levi, "True instruction was in his mouth, and nothing false was found on his lips." And he "turned many from iniquity." Many, not a few.

explanations.answer: He is the messenger of the LORD of Hosts
explanations.explanation: That's it. The LORD says, "people should seek instruction from his mouth, because he is the messenger of the LORD of Hosts." The priest isn't passing along his own opinions. He's carrying word from the LORD.

explanations.answer: He is the guardian of the house of the LORD
explanations.explanation: That sounds like a priest, but it's not the reason the verse gives. The LORD says people should seek instruction from his mouth "because he is the messenger of the LORD of Hosts." Messenger is the reason.

explanations.answer: He is the firstborn of the tribe of Levi
explanations.explanation: The verse doesn't mention birth order. The LORD says people should seek instruction from a priest's mouth "because he is the messenger of the LORD of Hosts." What matters is the message he carries, not where he sits in the family.

Stumble is right. The LORD says, "you have departed from the way, and your instruction has caused many to stumble." That's the danger of bad instruction. People trust the one teaching, and then they trip.
Boast isn't the word. The LORD says, "your instruction has caused many to stumble." It's about people tripping, not bragging. Their instruction led folks off the way.

Mourn isn't in the verse. The LORD says, "your instruction has caused many to stumble." Stumbling is about people losing their footing because of what they were taught. Nothing in the text says they cried.
The text says the opposite. The LORD tells the priests, "You have violated the covenant of Levi." They've departed from the way. They haven't kept it.
False is right. The LORD says, "You have violated the covenant of Levi." Right before that He says they "have departed from the way." So no, they haven't kept it.

Partiality is right. The LORD says they "have not kept My ways, but have shown partiality in matters of the law." In matters of the law, they played favorites. That's a long way from the priest Levi, who had nothing false on his lips.

Mercy would have been a lovely thing to find here, but it isn't what the verse says. The LORD says they "have not kept My ways, but have shown partiality in matters of the law." The word is partiality.

Patience isn't what the LORD names. He says the priests "have not kept My ways, but have shown partiality in matters of the law." That means they favored some people over others. The word is partiality.
